topic: blowing an even wide bowl from a clean gather and getting the annealing cycle right

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: pirometr optyczny na glory hole

base: I am blowing a wide bowl in the studio and the gathers keep coming out uneven.
A tall vase from last week sits on the bench, cracked right across its base.
I use an optical pyrometer on the glory hole, because the colour alone misleads me badly.
The glass runs thick on one side of the bowl and thin on the other.
Should I fix the gathering first, or work on how I open the piece out?
Fix the gather first, because every later shaping step inherits whatever thickness you started with.
An uneven gather never corrects itself, and marvering only hides the fault for a moment.
Turn the pipe steadily as you dip, and pull out along the same line each time.
Only once the gather runs true should you think about opening the bowl at all.
I slowed the turn and the gathers are far more even than they were before.
The pyrometer shows eleven forty in the glory hole, which seems low for this work.
The glass stiffens on the pipe before I have finished opening the rim out.
Do I raise the furnace, or simply reheat more often as I work?
Reheat more often, since running the glory hole hotter will scorch the surface of your bowl.
Eleven forty is perfectly workable for a wide form if you go back frequently.
Short reheats keep the whole piece at one temperature and prevent local stiffening.
A rim opened while one side is cooler will always run out of round.
Short reheats worked, and the rim opened round for the first time yesterday.
The pyrometer sat near eleven forty throughout and the surface stayed bright and clean.
That cracked vase on the bench came out of the annealer split at the base.
Is that a cooling fault, or did I chill the foot while working it?
A split base almost always means the annealing cycle ran down too quickly for the thickness.
Thick feet hold heat long after the walls have given theirs up entirely.
Hold the annealer at its soak temperature for an hour longer than you think necessary.
Then drop the heat slowly, no faster than twenty degrees in an hour.
I extended the soak by an hour and dropped the heat far more slowly.
The last three bowls came out of the annealer without a mark on them.
The rims are round and the walls run evenly from the foot upward.
Should I now try a colour overlay, or master the plain form for longer?
Master the plain form, because colour hides nothing and shows every fault twice over.
An overlay adds a second glass with its own expansion and its own habits.
Mismatched expansion cracks the piece weeks later, long after it has left the annealer.
Blow thirty plain bowls first, and the overlay will give you far less trouble.
I have blown twenty plain bowls and the last eight are almost identical.
My arms ache and the whole thing has begun to feel oddly automatic.
A friend wants to buy a set of six for her table this autumn.
Is there anything I should change when making a matched set rather than singles?
Make nine or ten, then choose the best six and put the rest aside.
Matching by eye is far easier than matching by measurement in hot glass.
Blow them on the same day, so the furnace and your hands stay consistent.
Anneal the whole set together, and they will hold their shape for a lifetime.
